main_damage_causes: Compression of Slughorn's self-serving, transactional social machinery (Slug Club train scene absent; Dumbledore's spider-web analysis condensed) leaves his moral complexity underexplored, making him warmer and less calculating than the book intends

Inversion of emotional agency in the Hagrid's hut memory-extraction scene (Francis the fish replaces Harry's frontal emotional assault), softening both Harry's calculated ruthlessness and the depth of Slughorn's resistance, and reducing the moral complexity of the scene's central transaction
Insufficient establishment of Slughorn's sustained wartime cowardice undermines the payoff of his eventual bravery in the Battle of Hogwarts, weakening his redemptive arc

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Slughorn's sitting room) — Dumbledore restores the room alone
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 5-8 establish that Dumbledore and Slughorn stand back-to-back and restore the room together in one identical sweeping motion — a small but telling moment of collegial equality and Slughorn's genuine competence as a wizard.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Dumbledore restores the room entirely on his own with a single wand movement. Slughorn is passive, a spectator to the repair.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The joint restoration in the book quietly signals that Slughorn is a peer-level wizard, not merely a comic subordinate. His absence from the repair subtly diminishes his stature as a powerful, capable wizard, which matters because his later resistance to Dumbledore is more credible when he is presented as an equal.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Slughorn's sitting room) — Slughorn's self-satisfied pride in his own cleverness is flattened
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 2, 4, 18 establish Slughorn's character texture through proud self-contradiction: he grumbles about being discovered yet can't resist boasting ('Two. Didn't hear my Intruder Charm go off... Still, I added the finishing touches to my upholstery'). He is vain about his own ingenuity even while complaining.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Slughorn's dialogue in the sitting room is compressed. The film keeps the basic situation but strips out his proud, half-irritable, half-boastful commentary on his own preparations (the two-minute warning, the Intruder Charm, the precise upholstery timing). He becomes simply reluctant rather than reluctant-and-vain.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Slughorn's specific brand of vanity — taking pride in his own cleverness even when it has failed him — is a defining character note. It is what makes him sympathetic and comic simultaneously. The film's compression removes this self-revealing texture, making him a more generic frightened old man rather than the particular, self-satisfied creature Rowling constructs.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (sitting room) — Slughorn's comment on Muggle-borns lacks Harry's cold pushback
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 44-47 show Slughorn saying 'Funny how that sometimes happens' about Muggle-borns being talented, and Harry coldly replying 'Not really.' This is a sharp, character-defining moment: Harry refuses to soften Slughorn's casual condescension, and Slughorn is startled enough to over-explain himself.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Slughorn makes his 'even more impressive when one considers she was Muggle-born' remark, and Harry replies 'One of my best friends is Muggle-born. She's the best in our year.' Slughorn's defensive back-pedalling follows, but Harry's cold, pointed 'Not really' — the rebuke — is absent. Harry is less adversarial.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Harry's 'Not really' is a small but precise moment establishing that Harry will not perform warmth toward Slughorn when Slughorn says something he finds offensive. It shades Harry's eventual 'collecting' relationship with Slughorn as wary rather than straightforwardly charmed. Its absence makes Harry seem more passive and Slughorn's prejudice less noted.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (sitting room) — Dumbledore's character analysis of Slughorn is moved to Scene 4 (exterior street) and significantly condensed
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 76-78 have Dumbledore deliver an extended, precise analysis of Slughorn: his love of comfort, the famous and successful, his 'Slug Club' methodology, his role as a spider at the center of a web, and the explicit warning that Slughorn will try to 'collect' Harry as the jewel of his collection. Dumbledore also frames this explicitly as putting Harry 'on his guard.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4 gives a compressed version: 'You are talented, famous and powerful — everything Horace values. Professor Slughorn is going to try to collect you, Harry. You would be his crowning jewel.' The spider metaphor, the web, the detailed mechanism of the Slug Club, and the explicit moral warning are absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Dumbledore's full analysis functions as a hermeneutic key for reading Slughorn throughout the film. Without the spider/web framing and the detail of how Slughorn 'reaps benefit in return,' the audience loses the precise moral complexity that makes Slughorn interesting: he is not simply vain, he is a calculated networker whose warmth is always transactional. The film's compressed version tells us the conclusion without the mechanism.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 17 (Slughorn's office after dinner party) — 'The Shelf' conversation replaces train compartment Slug Club scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 96-127 establish the Slug Club through a richly populated train compartment scene: multiple invitees, Slughorn's interrogation style, his reaction to Neville, his probing of Harry about the Ministry, Ginny's inclusion for hexing Zacharias Smith, Zabini's contemptuous report back to Malfoy. This is the audience's first full view of Slughorn as a social operator in action.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The train compartment scene is entirely absent. Instead, a dinner party in Slughorn's office (Film Scene 15-17) performs some of the same function but with different texture. Slughorn's one-on-one conversation with Harry about 'the shelf' replaces the ensemble scene. The film's Slughorn is more intimate and less nakedly transactional in this setting.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The train scene is the primary demonstration of Slughorn's Slug Club methodology in action — his coldness to Belby when Belby can't deliver on his uncle, his enthusiasm for McLaggen's Ministry connections, the way he passes over Ron entirely. Without it, the audience understands Slughorn abstractly (via Dumbledore's compressed description) rather than seeing his behaviour empirically. This reduces the moral edge of his characterisation.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 17 (Slughorn's office after party) — Slughorn raises Voldemort/Tom Riddle unprompted and frames him as 'not unlike you'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book never has Slughorn voluntarily open a discussion of Tom Riddle with Harry. Slughorn is consistently avoidant on this subject; Harry must work to raise it, and when he does (book scene 332) Slughorn freezes and flees. Slughorn's evasiveness about Riddle is fundamental to his characterisation and to the plot's tension.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In Film Scene 17, after the party, Slughorn volunteers: 'When I first met young Mr. Riddle, he was simply a quiet, albeit brilliant, boy committed to becoming a first-rate wizard. Not unlike the others I've known. In fact, not unlike... you.' He opens the subject of Riddle himself, unasked, and frames the comparison to Harry.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This inversion is damaging because it removes Slughorn's consistent, defining avoidance of all things Riddle-related. In the book, Slughorn's guilt and shame manifest as total silence on the subject; he will not go near it. The film's Slughorn raising Riddle voluntarily contradicts the psychological logic of his shame and makes his later refusal to give Harry the memory feel less deeply rooted and more arbitrary.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 22 (Slughorn's classroom, Harry's first attempt) — Harry mimics Riddle's exact approach to ask about Horcruxes
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 332 has Harry simply and directly ask 'Sir, I wondered what you know about... about Horcruxes?' after staying behind. Harry uses a straightforward approach, softened by the goodwill from the bezoar lesson, and Slughorn freezes and flees. The book version is a failed attempt that establishes the difficulty of the task.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 22 has Harry deliberately mimic Riddle's exact phrasing and approach ('I was in the library the other night, in the Restricted section... something about a bit of rare magic... he's not like you, he might misunderstand'). Slughorn recognises the echo, explicitly says 'Dumbledore put you up to this,' and the attempt fails. The scene foregrounds Harry's calculation rather than his directness.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Having Harry deliberately echo Riddle's manipulation is a characterisation choice that sits awkwardly with the book's Harry, who succeeds with Slughorn ultimately through emotional honesty and Felix-guided instinct, not through calculated mimicry of Voldemort. It also slightly undermines the emotional logic of the Hagrid's hut scene, where Harry's sincerity is meant to be what finally breaks through.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 22 (Slughorn's classroom) — Slughorn's bezoar-lesson context is absent; no extended failed-attempt period shown
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 332-415 show Harry making multiple failed attempts over weeks to get the memory: he tries after class, knocks on Slughorn's door twice, hears a gramophone through the door, and Slughorn actively avoids being alone with him. This extended failure period establishes the difficulty of the task and Slughorn's determination to avoid it.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses this to a single classroom attempt (Film Scene 22) and then the Ron love-potion visit (Film Scene 23-24), with Slughorn dodging Harry in a corridor moment (Film Scene 26). The texture of repeated failure over weeks is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The extended failure period in the book establishes that Slughorn's guilt is deep and his resistance is real — it is not merely shyness. The film's compression makes his eventual surrender feel less hard-won and reduces the dramatic weight of the Hagrid's hut scene as the culmination of a long campaign.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 28-30 (Greenhouse / Hagrid's hut) — Slughorn at greenhouse stealing Tentacula leaves replaces vegetable patch / twilight herb-picking scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 456-460 show Slughorn collecting herbs with Professor Sprout at twilight for legitimate academic purposes (third-year lessons). Harry finds him there by Felix-guided instinct. Slughorn is engaged in ordinary professional activity and is surprised by Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 28 shows Slughorn furtively stealing Tentacula leaves from a greenhouse — leaves worth 'ten galleons a leaf to the right buyer.' He is caught in a petty, mildly corrupt act. Harry uses this to his advantage, leveraging Slughorn's embarrassment to engineer the walk to Hagrid's.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film's choice to show Slughorn actively stealing (rather than legitimately collecting) deepens his venality at a moment when the narrative is about to ask the audience to feel emotionally moved by his guilt and his love for Lily. Having him caught pilfering just before the emotional climax of the film slightly cheapens his character. The book's Slughorn is self-serving but not petty-criminal; the distinction matters for the emotional register of what follows.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 30 (Hagrid's hut, night) — The 'Francis the fish' speech replaces Harry's direct account of his parents' deaths
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 522-553 show Harry deliberately and emotionally recounting the night his parents died — his father stepping over, his mother refusing to move, Voldemort laughing — in order to break Slughorn's resistance. The approach is emotionally frontal: Harry uses Slughorn's love for Lily as a lever, and the guilt of the memory is invoked through the specific horror of what Harry tells him. Harry says explicitly 'Be brave like my mother.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 30 introduces 'Francis the fish' — a story Slughorn tells voluntarily about a fish Lily gave him as a gift, whose disappearance marked the day she died. This is a film invention. The emotional architecture shifts: Slughorn volunteers his grief first, then Harry says 'she died for you too' and 'be brave like my mother.' The dynamic is Slughorn opening himself rather than Harry forcing the opening.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Francis fish story is the film's most significant addition to Slughorn's characterisation. While it is emotionally effective, it structurally changes who bears the emotional agency in the scene. In the book, Harry is the active agent — he is deliberately, coldly deploying the story of his parents' murder as a tool, guided by Felix. In the film, Slughorn opens the wound himself. This softens both Harry's calculated ruthlessness (which is important to his character at this stage) and Slughorn's resistance (which cracks more from his own sentiment than from Harry's pressure). The book's version is more morally complex for both characters.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 25 (Hospital wing) — 'I've always cherished my students. They're my life' replaces Slughorn's paralysis and uselessness during the poisoning
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 359-363 show Slughorn as 'paralysed by shock' and 'spluttering' while Ron convulses and turns blue. He is useless in the crisis — Harry has to act entirely on his own, sprinting to Slughorn's potions kit while Slughorn stands mouth agape. Afterward, 'Slughorn ran for help' is the extent of his contribution.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 25 gives Slughorn the line 'I've always cherished my students. They're my life...' as an emotional beat in the hospital wing, framing him as a man of deep feeling. The film's hospital wing scene is generally warmer toward Slughorn.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Slughorn is genuinely useless in the poisoning crisis — a small but telling detail that shows the limits of his self-regard. His paralysis is not cruelty but a kind of self-protective shutdown that is consistent with his character. The film's warmer hospital wing framing, while not dishonest, softens this edge and begins the process of rehabilitating Slughorn slightly too early and too easily.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 19 (Christmas party) — Malfoy gate-crash is handled by Snape alone; Slughorn's 'I did know your grandfather' moment is absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 275-283 show Slughorn allowing Malfoy to stay at the party ('It's Christmas... we'll forget any punishment') and then saying 'I did know your grandfather, after all.' This is a specific character note: Slughorn's social reflexes override his better judgment, and he extends hospitality to Malfoy on the basis of family connections even at a moment when Malfoy's family is compromised.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In Film Scene 19, Malfoy admits he was gate-crashing and Snape immediately steps in: 'I'll escort him out.' Slughorn barely registers. The 'I did know your grandfather' line and Slughorn's social-reflex hospitality are absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The small exchange with Malfoy at the party is a precise illustration of Slughorn's weakness: his network-reflex is so ingrained that he extends it even to Death Eater families at a wartime Christmas party. Its removal is a minor but real loss of the behavioural specificity that makes Slughorn's character so precisely observed.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 (Great Hall, feast) — Slughorn introduced without any independent characterisation moment
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: By the time of the Hogwarts feast in the book, the reader has already spent a substantial scene with Slughorn at the house in Budleigh Babberton, seen him operate, and heard Dumbledore's analysis. The feast introduction is redundant characterisation.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's feast introduction (Slughorn stands, belly casting a shadow) is physically accurate but brief. However, the film lacks the train compartment scene (see above) that would have given the audience an independent view of Slughorn in action before he is framed by Dumbledore's commentary.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor in isolation, but this compounds the loss of the train scene: the audience's only substantial independent view of Slughorn operating as a social networker comes from the dinner party scene, which is more intimate and less revealing of his transactional coldness than the train compartment. The cumulative effect is a Slughorn who is warmer and less calculating than the book intends.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film — Slughorn's self-serving avoidance during the war (hiding in Muggle houses, refusing to commit) is not dramatised beyond the opening scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 26-27, 53-57 establish Slughorn's moral position at length: he has been running for a year, using Freezing Charms on burglar alarms, squatting in Muggle houses, and refuses Hogwarts because he doesn't 'personally fancy the mortality rate.' Harry explicitly calls this out against the memory of Sirius living on rats in a cave. This cowardice is central to Slughorn's arc: his eventual bravery at the Battle of Hogwarts is meaningful because it contradicts his established character.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The opening scene establishes that Death Eaters have been trying to recruit Slughorn, but the full extent of his cowardly self-exile and Harry's contemptuous comparison to Sirius are absent. The film does not establish the depth of his prior moral failure.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Slughorn's arc from cowardly self-preservation to fighting Voldemort alongside McGonagall and Kingsley requires the audience to understand how far he has come. The film establishes that he was hiding but not the sustained, calculated, self-serving nature of that hiding. When Slughorn fights in the Battle of Hogwarts (film), the contrast is less powerful because the baseline cowardice has not been fully established.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film — Slughorn fighting Voldemort (Battle of Hogwarts) is present in the book corpus (book scenes 658, 661) but the film corpus does not include the battle sequence
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 658 and 661 show Slughorn duelling Voldemort alongside McGonagall and Kingsley, and being blasted backward when Voldemort's fury explodes at Bellatrix's death. This is the payoff of his arc: the self-serving coward stands and fights.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus provided does not include the Battle of Hogwarts sequence, so this cannot be scored directly. However, the absence of the established cowardice baseline (see above) means that even if the battle moment is present in the film, it carries less weight.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The incomplete establishment of Slughorn's cowardice early in the story means his climactic courage in the battle — which is the resolution of his character arc — is narratively underprepared. This is a structural damage to his arc even if the beat itself is present in the film.
